title: How Much Is a Second Head Worth?
text: Back to the drawer of biased coins. Coin A comes up heads three times out of four, and B once out of four. I picked one of them at random. I toss it, it comes up heads, and your bet on A goes from one half to three quarters. You ask me to toss the same coin again. I cover the result with my hand. Before you look, tell me something. If it came up heads again, will that second head be worth as much as the first? Coin A still comes up heads with probability 3 / 4 , and B with probability 1 / 4 . In that sense nothing has changed. But the first head already moved half the probability that belonged to B over to A’s column. How much is left for the second head to move? I lift my hand. Heads. At 32 tables we expect 16 coins of each type. Of the tables that see heads on the first toss, 12 will have A and 4 will have B, on average. If only those tables toss again, we expect 9 of the 12 tables with A and 1 of the 4 with B to see a second head. Each square represents one table in the expected counts. Colored squares show heads on the first toss. Dark squares show heads on the second toss as well. We started with one table holding A for every table holding B. After the first head there were three to one. After the second, nine to one. In that sense the two heads did exactly the same thing. Each tripled the odds in favor of A. Now read A’s column as a fraction of the tables still in the room. It went from 1 / 2 to 3 / 4 and then to 9 / 10 . The first head multiplied the probability of A by 3 / 2 , the second by 6 / 5 . If we used the first factor twice, we would get ( 3 / 4 ) ( 3 / 2 ) = 9 / 8 . We have just put more than 100% of the probability on a single coin. Where did our prediction change without our noticing? What Would It Take to Change My Mind? We can predict that change. I ask someone who knows they have coin A for the probability of heads. I ask you, too. If heads comes up, A gains probability whenever it predicted heads better than you did. To measure the gain, divide the new bet by the old one. Doubling a bet of ten centavos and doubling a bet of forty then give the same factor of two. For positive p ( x ) and p ( y ) , equating the two prices for the ticket gives W ( x , y ) = p ( y ∣ x ) p ( y ) = p ( x ∣ y ) p ( x ) . The left side tells us how much our bet on y changed. The right side compares two predictions for x . The ratios agree because the ticket that pays for x and y has a single price. On the first toss, the person holding A gave heads probability 3 / 4 and you gave it 1 / 2 . On the second toss, they still gave it 3 / 4 . And you? Among the 16 tables that saw heads on the first toss, we expected 10 to see it again. You were already giving probability 10 / 16 = 5 / 8 to the outcome under my hand. That’s where the 6 / 5 comes from. If h is the history already written in the notebook, the factor for its next line is p ( x ∣ y , h ) / p ( x ∣ h ) . Notice that the history enters both predictions. If I handed you a photograph of the first toss and told you it was a photograph, you and the person holding A could both predict with certainty which side it would show. The factor would be 1 / 1 . Can I promise to raise my bet on A whatever happens on the second toss? The average would go up, too. Here a head takes us to 9 / 10 and a tail brings us back to even odds. With the weights we had before looking, ( 5 / 8 ) ( 9 / 10 ) + ( 3 / 8 ) ( 1 / 2 ) = 3 / 4 . The books balanced before I even lifted my hand. Would you like to try the calculation on a particularly unlikely observation? At each table I put an envelope numbered from 000 to 999. I draw the number uniformly, independently of the coin. I open yours. It’s 731. Before I opened it, you would have given that number one chance in a thousand. If I had told you beforehand that your coin was A, you would have given it the same one chance in a thousand. We can put the envelope back in the drawer without changing the bet. Now I change one instruction. At tables that get A, I draw the envelope from the five hundred odd numbers. At tables that get B, I draw from the five hundred even ones. The two coins are still equally likely. What chance do you give 731 before you know the letter? Still one in a thousand. And when it turns up? Given coin A, 731 had one chance in five hundred. The factor in favor of A is two, just enough to take its probability from 1 / 2 to one. All I changed between the two games was how the number related to what you wanted to find out. A notebook that kept only a histogram of the numbers would look the same in both. The Price of a Look If someone charges us to open the envelope, we have to decide how much to pay before we know the result. Let me suggest a unit for keeping score. At the end of the round, I reveal the letter. If you had assigned certainty to the letter that came up, you pay nothing. If you had given it one half, you pay one point. If you had given it half of a half, you pay two. What would it cost to have given the right letter one eighth? Imagine I reveal the answer in two stages. You gave the first answer probability 1 / 2 and, knowing it, gave the second probability 1 / 4 . Getting the pair right meant getting through both filters. The probability you assigned the pair was 1 / 8 . I can hand you a single bill for three points or two bills, one for a point and one for two. You pay the same amount. That’s what I want the logarithm for. It counts the halvings between certainty and your bet. For 1 / 8 there are exactly three. For a bet between 1 / 4 and 1 / 2 , the scale reads somewhere between one and two. In mathematical notation, if r = 2 − c , the charge is c = − log 2 r . We chose two as the base because we wanted to charge one point per halving. Now work out what a look is worth. If seeing the face doubled your bet on the letter that eventually came up, you saved yourself one halving, whatever your starting bet. Tripling should likewise be worth the same wherever you start. That’s why we care about the factor by which the bet changed. Your saving is the charge before looking minus the charge afterward, − log 2 p ( y ) ⏟ before − [ − log 2 p ( y ∣ x ) ] ⏟ after = log 2 p ( y ∣ x ) p ( y ) = log 2 W ( x , y ) . You can even come out behind. If I drew B and happened to toss heads, you lowered your bet on the coin I’m about to show you from 1 / 2 to 1 / 4 . Peeking at that head cost you an extra point. This happens in a quarter of the rounds if we include the mirror case where A comes up tails. In the other three quarters you raise the probability of the right letter from 1 / 2 to 3 / 4 . The average saving is ( 3 / 4 ) log 2 ( 3 / 2 ) + ( 1 / 4 ) log 2 ( 1 / 2 ) , about 0.189 points. If the house charges 0.2 points for a peek, on average you pay more than you save. This expected saving is the mutual information , measured in bits when we take logarithms to base two. Each outcome and hypothesis enter as a pair, with their joint probability as the weight, I ( X ; Y ) = ∑ x , y : p ( x , y ) > 0 p ( x , y ) log 2 W ( x , y ) . We could also work out what we expect to pay before observing and subtract what we expect to pay afterward. Imagine a hundred rounds with your bet on A set at q . In about 100 q of them, you’d pay the charge for the probability you gave A. In the rest you’d pay for the probability you gave B. Divide the bill by a hundred rounds and you get the theoretical average charge h ( q ) = − q log 2 q − ( 1 − q ) log 2 ( 1 − q ) , the entropy of a binary bet. At even odds, h ( 1 / 2 ) = 1 bit. When we know the answer, the letter that will come up has probability one and the charge is zero. The Best Question to Ask the Coin We still don’t know which box was picked, Ordinary or Double. But we did see a head. If it was the Double box, we’re holding the two-headed coin. Which is worth more to us now: putting the coin back and drawing again from the same box, tossing the coin on the table again, or simply turning it over? If we put it back and draw again, each face remains equally likely in both boxes. One bit of uncertainty remains. If we turn it over, a tail on the other side identifies the Ordinary box and a head identifies the Double box. Our next bet on the right box will have probability one. If we toss the same coin again, half the tables have the Double box and another head is certain there. Of the half with the Ordinary box, half will see a tail. So a tail occurs at 1 / 4 of all tables and settles the question. Among the 3 / 4 that see a head, the fraction with the Double box will be ( 1 / 2 ) / ( 3 / 4 ) = 2 / 3 . After the toss our average charge for naming the box will be ( 3 / 4 ) h ( 2 / 3 ) points, since a tail made the answer certain. Of the three things you could do, the first is worth zero bits, the second 1 − ( 3 / 4 ) h ( 2 / 3 ) ≃ 0.311 bits, and the third one bit. Compare the extremes. When we put the coin back, there’s a one-half chance of seeing heads. When we turn it over, there’s also a one-half chance of seeing heads. The two actions give the same histogram of faces. Only one lets us find out which box we have. Before Asking for One More Observation Once it arrives. Compare what the hypothesis predicted for the outcome to what you predicted before looking. The ratio multiplies the probability of the hypothesis. If you can still choose what to observe. Imagine the outcomes each hypothesis would produce. Averaging log 2 W ( x , y ) over those possibilities tells you what it’s worth to look before betting, when we use the logarithmic charge. Who told us that coin A comes up heads on three tosses out of four?

title: Who Told Us How the Coin Works?
text: I was the one who told you that coin A comes up heads three times out of four. Today I brought the coins but left the instructions at home. That was the sheet that said how often each type was picked and how often it came up heads. We toss the coin and see a head. Should you raise your bet on A? Until we know which coin tends to give us more heads, we haven’t even settled which way the bet should move. I did bring something to put in place of the numbers I erased. It’s yesterday’s notebook. At the start of each round the experimenter picked a type of coin, A or B, at random. He tossed that same coin twice and revealed its type. Tomorrow he’ll play again, only this time he’ll keep the letter hidden until we’ve placed our bet. You can take the notebook home. What would you do with it? Here are yesterday’s eighty rounds. I chose the numbers so we could do the experiment by hand. Each entry counts the rounds with that many heads and the letter shown. The middle column includes both orders in which one head and one tail might have come up. Type revealed 0 heads 1 head 2 heads Total A 4 12 24 40 B 24 12 4 40 Total 28 24 28 80 Before counting heads, I’d ask the person who filled the notebook a question. Why are there forty coins of each type? If he deliberately set aside forty of each for me, the fifty-fifty split came from whoever put the sample together. Here the answer is different. The experimenter drew the type afresh each round, with no quotas, just as he’ll do tomorrow. Now I can use the last column to estimate the frequency of A in the round I care about. I would have read exactly the same numbers off the page in either case. A Program That Can Make Up a Round Imagine you wanted to build an imitation of the game. Your program has to supply the two faces and, at the end, be able to open its hand and reveal the letter. It could start by drawing A with probability π and B with probability 1 − π . If it draws A, it uses the rate θ A for heads. If it draws B, it uses θ B . So far we can print the first face. What should the program do to print the second? Let’s tell it to use the same rate and draw again, independently of the first draw. A short instruction. It says that once we know the type and its rate, the prediction for the next face stays the same whatever came up on the first toss. We also have to decide which rounds we can pool. An A drawn tomorrow has to have the same rate of heads as the A coins whose behavior we’re studying today. That’s how a notebook full of old coins earns the right to tell us something about a new one. Write Y for the letter and X for the faces. The program assigns each round the probability p θ ( x , y ) = p θ ( y ) p θ ( x ∣ y ) , where θ collects the three numbers we need to fit. It knows, for instance, that the chance of writing down A and two heads is π θ A 2 . If I promise one real for A and two heads, I have to give the same ticket the same price whichever way I count. But who gave me the right to use θ A 2 as the probability of two heads? The pricing rule says nothing about squaring a number. I was the one who told the program to make two independent draws after choosing A. When we fit the joint distribution of the faces and letters to the notebook, we’re doing generative learning . We can ask the program to produce a new notebook and see how well what comes out resembles what we brought back from the table. Can I Take the Pairs Apart? Cut each of the forty records for A in half. For the moment, leave the two pieces from each round side by side. How many heads do we have? The four rounds in the first column contribute none. The twelve in the middle contribute twelve. The twenty-four in the last column contribute forty-eight. That’s sixty heads and twenty tails. For a candidate value u of A’s rate of heads, the probability of those records contains sixty factors of u and twenty factors of 1 − u . Grouping the records in the table introduces a factor that’s the same for every candidate. We can compare them using just L ( u ) = u 60 ( 1 − u ) 20 . Imagine a knob that controls how often the program produces heads. Set it at u = 1 / 2 and it imitates a fair coin. Leave the eighty pieces where they are and turn only the knob. The height of the curve L ( u ) tells you how much that setting favors the record on the table. That’s what we call the likelihood . At u = 0 the program could never have produced those sixty heads. At u = 1 it could never have produced the twenty tails. Somewhere between those ends there’s a peak. If you started in the middle, which way would you turn the knob? Nudge it from 0.50 to 0.51 . Each of the sixty factors for heads grows by 2% of what it was. Each of the twenty factors for tails shrinks by 2%. For a small enough nudge, the sixty heads pull harder. What if you were already at 0.90 ? The same change of one hundredth would add a little over 1% to each factor for heads but take 10% off each factor for tails. Twenty tails can now outweigh sixty heads. What makes them so heavy? You’ve left them very little probability to give up. I could multiply all eighty factors again at every turn. But I only want to know whether I went up or down. The logarithm preserves the order of the heights, so the peak stays above the same mark on the dial. And it saves me some work. We write ln u for the exponent that gives u when the base is e ≃ 2.718 . For instance, e 2 e 3 = e 5 . Multiplying sixty copies of u adds sixty copies of the exponent ln u . I can write the height on the new scale as ln L ( u ) = 60 ln u + 20 ln ( 1 − u ) . Imagine laying a straightedge against the curve. On the way up, its right end sits higher than its left. On the way down, it sits lower. Somewhere between the two, the straightedge lies level. To locate that mark on the dial, we can measure how much the height changes with each little turn of the knob. On the natural-log scale, the measurement has a simple interpretation. If a factor grows by 1%, its logarithm changes by ln ( 1.01 ) ≃ 0.00995 , very nearly 0.01 . The smaller the nudge, the better that approximation gets. A tiny turn δ increases each factor for heads by the fraction δ / u of what it was. Each factor for tails loses the fraction δ / ( 1 − u ) . Add the gains and losses, then divide by the size of the turn. In the limit as the turn gets smaller, that gives the slope, or derivative , of the curve. d d u ln L ( u ) = 60 u ⏟ gain on heads − 20 1 − u ⏟ loss on tails . Where the straightedge lies level, the gain on heads balances the loss on tails. Both pans carry the same weight. We have three times as many heads as tails. For the twenty tails to balance the heads, each tail must give up three times the fraction each head gains. That happens when the space 1 − u left for tails is one third of the space u given to heads. Divide the scale into four equal parts. Three go to heads, one to tails. We have u = 3 / 4 . To the left of that mark, the first term is larger. To its right, the second is larger. That’s how we know we’ve reached the maximum. Each point uses the same eighty slips of paper. The little line at the top shows the tangent where the gains on heads balance the losses on tails. For B there are twenty heads in eighty tosses. The same balance gives θ ̂ B = 1 / 4 . Of the eighty letters, forty are A, giving π ̂ = 1 / 2 . We have recovered the instruction sheet from Chapter 1 by maximum likelihood . If I bring another sample tomorrow, all three numbers might change. You still have A’s eighty slips on the table. Pick two rounds that each had a head and a tail. Swap one face from the first round with one from the other so you end up with a pair of heads and a pair of tails. You’ve made up a different history for the game. A’s row, which read 4 , 12 , 24 , would now read 5 , 10 , 25 . What would the program that estimates θ A notice? The same sixty heads and twenty tails are still on the table. If I handed you the two tables without saying which one I’d changed, you’d have exactly the same grounds for preferring any candidate u to any other in either table. We gave the program permission to forget which other face each head came with. What if I shuffle all eighty slips? I can still estimate the rate of heads. But see what I can no longer check without reconstructing the pairs from the original notebook. With θ ̂ A = 3 / 4 , the program expects one of each face in 2 ( 3 / 4 ) ( 1 / 4 ) = 3 / 8 of A’s rounds. The factor of two is there because either face can come first. The rates switch places for B, so the probability is still 3 / 8 . In a run of eighty rounds, the program expects thirty with one head. We counted twenty-four. A run can fluctuate, of course. But if the difference persists in fresh notebooks, I’ll know where to look. The generator’s books balance both for the heads and for the pairs it makes itself. Now we have a reason to keep the pairs that actually came out of the workshop. They let us discover that we chose the wrong generator even if we did every one of its calculations correctly. What Changes When We Open Our Hand? The next morning, the experimenter draws another coin from the drawer, covers its label and tosses it twice. Two heads. Using our estimates, the chance that the round would produce A and two heads was ( 1 / 2 ) ( 3 / 4 ) 2 = 9 / 32 . For B and two heads it was ( 1 / 2 ) ( 1 / 4 ) 2 = 1 / 32 . Among rounds with that outcome, what fraction carry the letter A? We get ( 9 / 32 ) / ( 9 / 32 + 1 / 32 ) = 9 / 10 . We made that bet holding the three estimates fixed. The experimenter opens his hand. It’s B. We can add the round to our training data. The letter he revealed is the label . When each training input comes with its label, we call this supervised learning . Our estimate of B’s rate of heads goes from 20 / 80 to 22 / 82 . We know the identity of the coin that just went back into the drawer. The new rate will help us bet on the next one. Perhaps you’d like to keep more than one setting for the program. Give each an initial weight and ask which would most readily have produced what you just saw. A candidate ( π , θ A , θ B ) gave the newly revealed row probability ( 1 − π ) θ B 2 . Of each candidate’s initial weight, keep only the fraction that would produce that row. Gather what survives across all settings. Each setting’s share of that total is your new bet on it. It’s the update from Chapter 1, now applied to parameters. When we got 9 / 10 , we chose to work with one estimated setting. The name generative comes from what we asked the program to describe. What the Cut-Up Slips Let Us Check To fit the rate. Once we assume a fixed rate and independent tosses given the type, we can count A’s heads and tails without keeping the pairs. To test the assumption. For this we need the pairs themselves. A notebook big enough to estimate the rate can be too small to test the instruction we wrote into the program. Go back to the original notebook. In twenty-four of the twenty-eight rounds with two heads, the letter was A. You count 24 / 28 . I offer 9 / 10 . On which line of the calculation did I give myself permission to change your fraction?

title: Two Ways to Read the Same Table
text: Two heads on the table, the letter still hidden. For R$ 8.80 I’ll sell you a ticket that pays ten reais if the coin is A and nothing if it is B. We can do this many times. If you care about your average gain, do you buy? The person who brought the generator reaches for a wallet. At 9 / 10 , the ticket is worth nine reais. The person who brought the notebook counts twenty-four A’s out of twenty-eight. By that estimate the ticket is worth R$ 8.57. The wallet stays in the pocket. If all I’d asked for was a letter, both would have said A. Lay the training notebook open on the table. Revealed type 0 heads 1 head 2 heads Total A 4 12 24 40 B 24 12 4 40 Total 28 24 28 80 Put your finger on the 24 in the first row. What else do you need to read to turn it into a probability? If you want the fraction of A rounds that gave two heads, read across the row and divide by forty. If you want the probability that the coin is A given two heads, read down the column and divide by twenty-eight. Your finger hasn’t moved. The question chose the denominator. The generator counted the other columns too and estimated each coin’s chance of heads. In forty rounds of each type, it expects 40 ( 3 / 4 ) 2 = 22.5 A rounds with two heads and 40 ( 1 / 4 ) 2 = 2.5 B rounds with two heads. The column it expects to see suggests 22.5 / ( 22.5 + 2.5 ) = 9 / 10 . The one we saw yesterday gives 24 / ( 24 + 4 ) = 6 / 7 . Didn’t we just insist on a single price for the same ticket? Before we toss, consider a ticket paying one real for A and two heads. In yesterday’s notebook we can count by row or by column, 40 80 24 40 = 24 80 = 28 80 24 28 . In the notebook the generator expects to produce, the two prices agree as well, 1 2 ( 3 4 ) 2 = 9 32 = 5 16 9 10 . The first calculation uses observed frequencies. The second builds the pair of tosses by assuming independence. To catch either learner contradicting itself, I’d have to get two prices from its own assumptions. To see which one makes the better purchase, I need fresh rounds. A bill that depends only on the letters Tomorrow, whenever I have to give an answer, I’ll already have seen both tosses. I can use the training rounds to fit the probability of the letter directly for each outcome I might be shown. Learning to predict Y from X this way is called discriminative learning . To see how it works, keep just the twenty-eight tickets in the last column and pick a probability q to announce for A. What would the notebook charge you for that choice? Suppose you announced q = 0.80 for A. Make two piles of tickets, the twenty-four A’s on one side and the four B’s on the other. Now give A an extra hundredth of probability. In the bigger pile, the charge on each of the twenty-four tickets goes down a little. Where did that hundredth come from? Out of the 0.20 you had set aside for B. The four tickets in that pile get more expensive. If you keep taking from B, which pile will eventually have the greater say in the bill? Use the scale from the last chapter. For a tiny nudge in q , the saving on each A depends on the size of the nudge relative to the bet q . For a B ticket, the extra charge depends on the nudge relative to what was left, 1 − q . At q = 0.80 , the twenty-four savings pull with a strength of 24 / 0.80 = 30 . The four extra charges pull back with a strength of 4 / 0.20 = 20 . It pays to go up. Try q = 0.90 . Now the savings add up to about 26.7 per unit of movement and the extra charges add up to 40. You’ve gone too far. We can write down what we just weighed. Each A costs − ln q and each B costs − ln ( 1 − q ) . Using natural logarithms just changes the units on the bill. This time the height of the curve is an expense. We’re looking for the bottom of the valley. If D is the total expense, its slope is D ( q ) = − 24 ln q − 4 ln ( 1 − q ) , D ′ ( q ) = − 24 q + 4 1 − q . At the balance point, 24 / q = 4 / ( 1 − q ) . There are six times as many A tickets as B tickets. For the two sides to weigh the same, A’s share of the probability must be six times B’s. Six parts out of seven gives q = 6 / 7 = 24 / 28 . Up to that point a nudge to the right reduces the bill. Beyond it, the bill goes up. Now we know why counting the letters gives precisely the cheapest bet in this notebook. We can do the same in the other columns. With zero heads, the cheapest bet on A is 4 / 28 = 1 / 7 . With one head, it is 12 / 24 = 1 / 2 . Our program would fit on the back of a large coin. Keep three fractions and look up the one for the column you’ve been given. But suppose I cover an entire column before training. You’ll have no fraction to look up for that column. What would you have to add to venture an answer anyway? How can we guess what’s in the covered column? Let’s look for a clue in the generator. With rates 3 / 4 and 1 / 4 , each head triples the odds in favor of A. Each tail divides them by three. Take one head and one tail and cross them both off the page. Your bet is back where it started. After you’ve crossed off every such pair, what’s left? With H heads and T tails, the difference s = H − T counts the multiplications by three that remain, or the divisions if it’s negative. Starting from odds r 0 , we end up at r 0 3 s . Imagine the marks 1 , 3 , 9 , 27 on a ruler for the odds. It costs exactly one extra head to move from one mark to the next. If I want equal steps in the notebook to cover equal distances on the ruler, where should I put those marks? Take their logarithms and they land at 0 , ln 3 , 2 ln 3 , 3 ln 3 . The difference now counts steps, each of length ln 3 . For a bet q on A, our final position is ln q 1 − q = ln r 0 + s ln 3 . A straight line appeared before we ever mentioned regression. The starting mark came from the odds before we saw the tosses. The step length came from the difference between the two coins. Let’s keep the ruler and let the notebook choose those two measurements. Call the starting mark β 0 and the step length β 1 . For a difference s we read v = β 0 + β 1 s . How do we get from a mark back to a probability? If it reads ln 3 , there are three parts A for one part B. The bet on A is three of the four parts. If the mark reads v , undoing the logarithm gives e v parts A for one part B. Divide by the total number of parts. Dividing the numerator and denominator by e v just counts the same parts in a different unit. This gives us logistic regression , q ( s ) = e v 1 + e v = 1 1 + e − v , v = β 0 + β 1 s . The labels will choose the coefficients. We supplied the requirement that the three bets fit on a single straight line on this scale. 1 You’ve seen the numbers in the last column. Cover it anyway. We want to know whether we were still free to choose the bet in that column once we’d agreed to use the line. The two visible columns have differences of − 2 and 0 . In the first, the odds in favor of A are four to twenty-four, or one to six. In the second they’re twelve to twelve, or one to one. Moving two units to the right multiplied the odds by six. Before you lift your finger, what will you write in the last column? We’re moving another two units. If the log odds lie on a straight line, we have to multiply by six again. One to one becomes six to one, giving a probability of 6 / 7 . You can lift your finger. The observed odds were indeed twenty-four to four. In this table the line through the two visible points also minimizes the loss in the third column. The height is zero at s = 0 and ln 6 at s = 2 , so the fitted coefficients are β ̂ 0 = 0 and β ̂ 1 = ( ln 6 ) / 2 . With the rates fitted by the generator, the slope was ln 3 . The two programs arrived at curves in the same family. One fitted rates that explain the tosses within each coin type. The other fitted the probabilities that the line assigns to the letters. We could also use Bayes to learn the line. Whenever a letter is revealed, we multiply the weight of each candidate line by the probability it gave that letter at that value of s . We then normalize across candidates. The training is still discriminative. The lines bet on the letter given the tosses. Let’s do a little damage to the notebook. Correct a single letter in the middle column from B to A. The bets in the outer columns still give heights of − ln 6 and ln 6 , but the odds in the middle are now thirteen to eleven. No straight line can meet all three requests at once. If we fit a single line to the eighty rounds, a correction in the middle can change the bet even in the two-heads column, where no letter changed. The same assumption that lets one column teach us about another can lead us astray when the relationship we imagined breaks down. Before you buy the ticket Read the denominator. Fitting the joint distribution lets us ask how each type produces the tosses. Fitting the conditional directly lets us ask which letter to expect given the tosses we’ve seen. For classification, both can arrive at the same shape of curve. Look for what was borrowed. The generator linked tosses through a common rate for each type. Logistic regression linked columns through the slope of a line. When an observation changes the prediction for a different input, look for the assumption that linked them. I’d seal both predictions and set aside whole rounds with fresh coins for testing. To decide whether to buy at R$ 8.80, I want to know whether A occurs in more than 88 % of rounds with two heads. To assess the probabilities throughout the game, I want the average log loss on new rounds. If I decided from the notebook used for training, I’d be letting the directly fitted model grade its own exam. So far, one head already favored A. If the first toss on its own tells us nothing and the second on its own tells us nothing either, is there any point in keeping both? A. Y. Ng and M. I. Jordan examine what happens when we fit classifiers through the joint distribution or directly through the conditional distribution in On Discriminative vs. Generative Classifiers (2001). ↩︎

title: What Does the Classifier Need to Remember?
text: I hand you a ticket and a pencil. The ticket came from one of two printers, A or B, chosen at random with equal chances. It has two windows covered by paper flaps. In each window the machine printed heads or tails. Your job is to identify the machine. Open the first flap. Heads. Half of A’s tickets show heads in the first window. For B it’s half as well. What’s your bet on A? Write 1 / 2 on the back. Now do me a favor. Since that head did nothing to change your bet, take your pencil and cross out the picture until you can’t see it anymore. If you’re still holding the pencil, wait a moment. There’s a difference between the printers. A chooses the first face at random and, nine times out of ten, copies it into the second window. B also chooses the first at random, but nine times out of ten it prints the opposite face in the second window. Those chances of copying are the same whether the first window shows heads or tails. Someone who sees only the second window will also find the same frequency of heads in both machines. Under A, for example, the first could have been a head and the machine copied it, or the first could have been a tail and the machine reversed it. Add them up and we have ( 1 / 2 ) ( 9 / 10 ) + ( 1 / 2 ) ( 1 / 10 ) = 1 / 2 . Under B the two copying and reversing probabilities simply trade places. Close the first flap without crossing out the picture. Before you open the other flap, write down two bets on A. If I show you another head, you’ll have seen a repeat. The odds in that case are nine to one in favor of A. Your bet on A will be 90 % . If I show you a tail, it will be 10 % . Now imagine the first picture had been tails. The back of your ticket would still say 1 / 2 , but you’d have to reverse the instructions for the second window. Open the second flap. Heads. Someone who just walked in and saw only that window gives A a probability of 1 / 2 . You give it 9 / 10 . When did you learn something from the first head? You could already show what it had taught you before opening the second flap. It was there in the two bets you just wrote down. A model that counts every head and misses the repeats Let’s give the problem to two learners. Neither knows the printing trick. Each gets a notebook with two hundred tickets whose origins we know. I’ve chosen counts that reproduce the proportions in the workshop exactly. As before, H stands for heads and T for tails, this time in the order of the two windows. Machine H H H T T H T T Total A 45 5 5 45 100 B 5 45 45 5 100 The first learner wants to make tickets like the ones it found. It measures the frequency of heads in each window for each machine. It gets 1 / 2 four times. If I order a hundred A tickets, it will draw the two faces independently at those rates. It expects to produce twenty-five H H tickets. A produced forty-five. If I order a hundred B tickets, it expects the same twenty-five. B produced five. Which of the four counts did it get wrong? It got them all right. The learner itself put the instruction to draw the faces independently into the program. When we use a generator like this for classification, we call it Naive Bayes . Here is the assumption we put in by hand, p ( x 1 , x 2 ∣ y ) = p ( x 1 ∣ y ) p ( x 2 ∣ y ) . Why would anyone agree to it? Add one more window to every pattern you already have. Each old pattern now has two possible continuations. Do that doubling for ten windows and we arrive at 2 10 = 1 , 024 patterns. If I give you the probabilities of 1,023 of them, you get the last one from what’s left over to make one. That’s 1 , 023 free numbers per machine. Our learner asks for ten rates of heads per machine, one for each window, and it gets to use every ticket to estimate every rate. If I know that each print head has its own independent randomizer, and that its settings stay fixed within each machine, I have a reason to try that shortcut. Add the two rows of the table. There are fifty tickets in each of the four columns. Anyone who checks the whole notebook for independence will find it. But there’s a vertical bar in the formula, with a y on its right. Stay in row A. After a head, the second window shows heads in 45 / 50 of the cases. After a tail, in 5 / 50 . The assumption the program needed fails precisely when we check it in the group it describes. We can write a different recipe for the generator. First draw the face on the left. Then draw whether the machine will copy it. To train that second draw, just add the two outer columns. Ninety of A’s hundred tickets repeat the first face, compared with ten of B’s hundred. On an order of a hundred A tickets, the new recipe expects 100 ( 1 / 2 ) ( 9 / 10 ) = 45 pairs marked H H . When it receives an unlabeled H H ticket, it assigns A a probability of 45 / ( 45 + 5 ) = 9 / 10 . We still have a generative model. What we changed was an assumption about the printer. What a multiplication puts into a model The second learner wants to estimate the probability of the letter directly from the faces. It writes + 1 for heads and − 1 for tails. It proposes a logistic regression in which the log odds of A are b 0 + b 1 x 1 + b 2 x 2 . Let’s try its formula without fitting a single coefficient. On an H T ticket, change the tail on the right to a head. The bet on A should go up from 1 / 10 to 9 / 10 . Make the very same change on a T T ticket. This time the bet should go down from 9 / 10 to 1 / 10 . Cover the left window in both calculations. Changing the right from − 1 to + 1 takes − b 2 out of the sum and puts + b 2 in its place. The change in log odds is 2 b 2 on both tickets. Which sign would you choose for b 2 ? The learner can keep collecting tickets. It will still need a sign that changes depending on the first window. I want an instruction that leaves the reading on the right alone when the left shows + 1 and reverses its sign when the left shows − 1 . Multiplying by the reading on the left does just that. The product z = x 1 x 2 gives + 1 for repeats and − 1 for mismatches. The odds in favor of A in those two groups are nine to one and one to nine. On the logarithmic ruler those marks lie at the same distance from zero, one on either side. Use z to choose the side and ln 9 to mark the distance. Fitting a logistic regression to these proportions gives ln p ( A ∣ z ) p ( B ∣ z ) = z ln 9 . The product is an interaction term . Multiply x 2 by x 1 and watch what happens to the contribution of a head on the right when you change the face on the left. That’s the change of sign we asked for. Even this fix involved a choice of our own. By supplying only z , we lumped H H together with T T . The program lost the freedom to give them different probabilities. So I’d keep the original faces in the next batch to check whether the distinction I erased can still safely be ignored. The generator and the logistic model agree on the letter for every ticket. Can I put away the generator and use logistic regression to plan production? On both machines, change the rate of heads in the first window from 1 / 2 to 0.8 , keeping the copying probabilities the same. For every hundred A tickets we now expect 72 pairs marked H H . For every hundred B tickets we expect eight. The classifier still gives A a probability of 72 / ( 72 + 8 ) = 9 / 10 on seeing H H . For the other patterns, too, the changed frequency of the first face cancels when we take the ratio between the machines. Anyone ordering a hundred A tickets has good reason to ask whether to expect 45 or 72 pairs of heads. The logistic model can price every bet on the letter correctly without discovering what I changed on the printer. Who chose the examples? I often tell my students that we do the modeling when we decide what assumptions we have to bring to the problem ourselves. The next two workshops want the same thing. Tomorrow an unlabeled ticket will arrive and someone will have to guess its origin. In which workshop would I start with each approach? In the first, it costs money to discover the letter. The workshop investigates only half the tickets with matching faces and one in ten of those with different faces. Within each group it chooses the tickets at random. Apply that procedure to our table. Of the hundred matching tickets, we expect to investigate fifty, of which 45 will be A’s. Of the hundred mismatches we expect to investigate ten, of which one will be an A. The expected audit counts put the share of matching tickets at 50 / 60 . On the conveyor belt it’s one half. If I used this file to generate another print run, I’d already be wrong on my first order. But the chance of A among the matches is still 45 / 50 , and among the mismatches it’s 1 / 10 . Sampling shrank each column without favoring either letter within it. I’d start with the discriminative approach because I understand why the proportions I need survived sampling. The decisive information came from whoever chose the tickets for inspection. In the other workshop I go to the two printers myself. I take a hundred tickets at random from A’s output and a hundred from B’s. Now I can estimate what each machine prints. My notebook is half A because I just decided it would be. On tomorrow’s shift only one ticket in ten will come from A. If the mechanic tells me the settings are staying put, I can carry over the rates I measured at the bench and use the production mix. A repeat still favors A by a factor of nine. Since the starting odds have fallen to one to nine, after a repeat my bet on A is 1 / 2 . Here I’d start with the generator. Stable settings are an assumption I’d want to be able to defend with the mechanic. The hundred tickets from each machine can’t make that promise on their own. You can also correct the bet of a calibrated discriminative model if you know the old mix, the new mix, and that the same stability holds. In practice, the choice depends on what I can justify about the next shift. To test my choice, I’d set aside a batch from the actual conveyor belt. If the job is to sort tickets, I’d uncover the labels to measure the cost of sending a ticket to the wrong bin. If it’s to plan the print run, I’d compare the number of tickets of each pattern with the quantities I’d promised the buyer. Before you erase a column What I need to find out. When sampling preserves the share of each letter within each pattern and my task is to identify the machine, I can fit that share directly. When I know each machine’s output and the mix for the next shift, I can put the prediction together from the pieces I measured. What I put in by hand. Drawing the two faces separately and representing them only by their product are different assumptions. One rules out dependence within each machine. The other asks for the same bet on two heads as on two tails. Back to your ticket. Can I build a reader with room to store only one bit? As it opens the first flap it writes heads or tails in that space. When it opens the second, it compares what it sees with what it stored, then replaces the first entry with the answer to the question same or different? Now it can cross out both faces and still bet on the machine. We had enough room from the beginning. What had to change between the two readings was the meaning of that one entry.

title: When Is Getting It Right Enough?
text: I have two groups of learners at the workshop, grading tickets. Whenever the two faces match, everyone writes A. One group thinks nine out of ten such tickets come from A. The other thinks six out of ten do. If the test asks only for the letter on each ticket, I can swap the two groups’ answer sheets and nobody will notice. You know a way to tell them apart. Walk back into the room with the ticket that costs R$ 8.80 and pays ten reais if the machine was A. One group expects to collect nine reais and buys it. The other expects six and passes. Suppose, though, that all the workshop wants is to route tickets into two drawers, and that a mistake costs the same in either direction. For that job, how much is it worth to distinguish two bets that open the same gate? What Do You Charge for a Right Answer? Let’s keep the faces, the labels, and even the form of the function we use to classify them. As in the last chapter, z = + 1 means the faces match, and z = − 1 means they differ. Our score will be f w ( z ) = w z . Give A the label y = + 1 and B the label y = − 1 . The symmetry of our workshop lets us use the same coefficient for both kinds of ticket. On matching faces, w = 0.4 gives A, and so does w = 4 . What would make one number earn its place over the other? Logistic regression has an answer. Its score measures the log odds of A. By the time we grade the test, though, we know which letter came up. A score of − 2 when the letter is B deserves as much credit as + 2 when the letter is A. We can turn the ruler around for the B tickets. Multiplying the score by the label y leaves the reading alone for A and reverses its sign for B. Call this reading in favor of the letter that actually came up m = y f w ( z ) . For both right answers in the example, m = 2 . What probability did the learner give the right letter? On the ruler we just turned around, the odds in its favor are e m to one. Of the 1 + e m parts, e m belong to that letter. Its share is therefore p r i g h t = 1 / ( 1 + e − m ) , as in the previous chapter. To work out the charge, look at the denominator. It tells you what you would have to multiply that share by to get back to one. The logarithm of that factor is the price we set in Chapter 2, this time in natural logarithm units, ℓ l o g ( m ) = − ln p r i g h t = ln ( 1 + e − m ) . Even a learner who got the letter right still owes something. Among the tickets with matching faces, the bill is smallest when we quote the fraction of A tickets in the pile, as we saw in Chapter 4. Nine A tickets and one B ticket call for odds of nine to one, or w = ln 9 . If the pile has six A tickets and four B tickets, the odds are three to two and the score drops to ln ( 3 / 2 ) . With no penalty, the fractions for the tickets with different faces are mirror images of these, so the same coefficient works for both groups. Let me propose another way to grade the test. I’ll charge one point for a tie, m = 0 . For a step in the right direction, I’ll take a point off the bill. For a step in the wrong direction, I’ll add a point. The bill has a floor. Once you reach m = 1 , I charge nothing more on that ticket. A right answer with m = 0.6 therefore costs 0.4 points and a wrong one with m = − 0.6 costs 1.6 . This rule is called the hinge loss , ℓ h ( m ) = max ( 0 , 1 − m ) . We call the product m the functional margin . Let’s see what the new bill does to those nine right answers. On both curves, a positive margin means the predicted letter is correct. For hinge loss, once m reaches 1 the charge for that example falls to zero. Put ten tickets with matching faces on the table, nine from A and one from B. At w = 0 the hinge bill comes to ten points. Move from zero to one. You take a point off nine tickets and pay an extra point on one. You still owe two points. Now suppose you want to go from one to two. Which of the nine right answers will still earn you a discount? None of them. The only bill that changes belongs to the wrong answer, and it goes up by one point. The loss is linear on each stretch, and moving to the negative side would favor the minority. The best place to stop is w = 1 . Trade three A tickets for three B tickets. You now have six against four. Up to w = 1 , the six discounts still cover the four extra charges. Beyond one, all that happens is that the four mistakes get more expensive. The best place is still w = 1 . I could hand you the winning coefficient, explain exactly how I chose it, and ask what I ought to pay for the next ticket. Could you tell whether I had the pile with nine A tickets or the one with six? The gate reads the positive sign and gives the same answer for both piles. Now suppose someone feeds the score of one through the logistic sigmoid and announces a probability of about 73 % for A. That gives us a price of R$ 7.31 for both piles. One pile suggests nine reais and the other suggests six. I could defend R$ 7.31 if I found that frequency in fresh tickets with the same score. But that promise took an extra assumption about what the number one meant. The hinge loss only charged us for the margin. Where the Margin Comes From To get to a support vector machine , or SVM, we have one more choice to make. The workshop inspector brings us a caliper. The gate now sorts parts by their measured diameter. In the batch we fit to, the largest B part measures 4.8 mm and the smallest A part measures 5.2 mm. Anything above the threshold goes to A. I set my threshold at 5.15 mm. You set yours at 5.00 mm. We test the parts one by one, and we both get every one right. Before placing an order for your gate or mine, what would you like to ask the inspector? He takes the part that measured 5.2 , lifts it out of the caliper, and clamps it again. Just changing its position, he tells us, can make two readings differ by as much as 0.10 mm. Now there is a difference between our two perfect scores. A second reading of 5.10 sends the part through my gate to B. At your gate it still has room to spare. The same reasoning works from the other side. Among the boundaries that got the whole batch right, the one at 5.00 mm gives the nearest part on either side the most clearance. The person who knew how much that clearance was worth was holding the caliper. Why didn’t we simply reward a high score on the right side? If our ruler is f ( 𝐮 ) = 𝐰 ⊤ 𝐮 + b , I can double 𝐰 and b without moving the boundary f = 0 by so much as a millimeter. The scores have doubled. The part is just as far from the boundary as before. To connect the two scales, imagine that walking one millimeter perpendicular to the boundary adds four points on the display. To pick up one point, you need to move a quarter of a millimeter. The norm ∥ 𝐰 ∥ plays the part of those four points per millimeter. Take the displacement along each axis, multiply it by its weight, and add the results. This measures how far you went in the direction of 𝐰 , scaled by its length. In that direction, perpendicular to the boundary, a distance d adds d ∥ 𝐰 ∥ to the score. The line where the score is + 1 therefore lies 1 / ∥ 𝐰 ∥ from the boundary. The line where it is − 1 lies just as far away on the other side. When we can give every example y i f ( 𝐮 i ) ≥ 1 , choosing the smallest norm ∥ 𝐰 ∥ gives us the widest strip. With our caliper, that puts the threshold halfway between the two nearest parts. But for a ticket with two heads, we know the very same input can carry either label, A or B. No straight line can put them on different sides. Let’s strike a bargain. We want to widen the strip and we’re willing to pay for the parts that fall inside it or on the wrong side. If I double the number of parts by copying each one, I want the average cost of the errors to stay the same. That’s why I divide the bill for the parts by n . On the other pan of the balance I choose to charge for the square of the norm. Doubling the scale makes that charge four times as large. I have made a choice about what the width of the strip is worth. With both charges included, the cost minimized by a linear soft-margin SVM is 1 n ∑ i = 1 n max { 0 , 1 − y i f ( 𝐮 i ) } + λ 2 ∥ 𝐰 ∥ 2 , λ > 0 . The first term is the charge we applied to our two piles. The second charges for scaling up the coefficients even when we leave the boundary exactly where it was. A larger λ puts more weight on the norm. The location of the boundary depends on the parts that reach the margin or violate it. Among them are the support vectors . The value w = 1 in our envelope example came from the loss alone. In fitting an SVM, the penalty has a say too. 1 At the workshop I would test the SVM if I wanted the sorting decision to hold up under repeated measurements and could justify the ruler I used to measure distance. If I give the machine both diameter and weight, changing grams to milligrams already changes the geometry of the raw data. Nobody learned anything new about the parts by changing units. It falls to me to decide what a step along each axis is worth. To check my choice, I would set aside parts of known origin and measure them again. The clearance I found on yesterday’s parts interests me only if it helps route the ones coming through today. Now change the job. We want to decide whether a part is worth inspecting. An inspection costs two reais and prevents a loss of ten reais if the part came from B. Call the risk of B at that measurement r . An inspection is worth doing when 10 r > 2 . At an inspection price of four reais, the cutoff moves from 20 % to 40 % . A part with a 30 % risk changes destination without anybody touching the caliper. Here I would start with logistic regression. I can take its risk estimate to the person who knows the prices. There is one detail. In the batch where A and B separated perfectly, who measured the risk for a 5.05 mm part? No part had that diameter. A steeper and steeper logistic curve can keep improving the fit to the letters in the batch. Before spending money on the strength of its number, I would find labeled parts near the decision threshold and check whether the announced risks match what happens. We can also learn to calibrate an SVM score. For that I would set aside labeled data from the population where I plan to use the score and measure the frequency of B there. Can We Learn When the Answer Stays the Same? Set both programs to w = 2 . Give each of them a ticket with matching faces that turns out to be an A. Both got it right. Now slide your finger to the right on the loss graph, from 2 to 2.01 . On the hinge curve, your finger traveled along the flat stretch. The logistic curve still slopes down. Just by looking, you can tell which learner has a reason to increase w after seeing this ticket. How much does it still stand to gain? At m = 2 , the logistic charge is about 0.1269 . At 2.01 it is 0.1257 . A step of one hundredth saved about 0.0012 points. The local slope must be close to − 0.12 points per unit of margin. We can understand the size of that number by looking at the bet. In ln ( 1 + e − m ) , the one stays put. If m increases by one hundredth, the term e − m gets multiplied by e − 0.01 , about 0.99 . It loses nearly a hundredth of itself. As we take smaller and smaller steps, the amount it loses per unit step approaches e − m itself. The logarithm measures that change relative to the total 1 + e − m . The slope is therefore ℓ ′ l o g ( m ) = − e − m 1 + e − m = − ( 1 − p r i g h t ) . The learner who put close to 88 % on the right letter still had nearly 12 % on the wrong side. That leftover share is what the ticket contributes to the adjustment. A gradient step tells us to move against the slope to bring the bill down. If η > 0 controls the step size, then, since m = w here, the ticket adds η / ( 1 + e 2 ) to w . On the hinge curve, a slope of zero adds zero. Suppose we also charge λ w 2 / 2 for the coefficient. Why does a large w feel a stronger pull back toward zero? Picture w 2 as the area of a square with side w > 0 . Extend the side a little and you add two strips of length w and a tiny corner that shrinks with the square of the step. The area grows at a rate of 2 w . Multiply by the rate we charge, λ / 2 , and you get a slope of λ w . That part subtracts η λ w from both updates. We can now tell how much of the turn of the dial came from the new letter and how much came from a charge that was already there. We could have made a different choice at the outset. For each kind of ticket, keep just the counts of A and B. When a new letter arrives, add one to its count. With the same notebook I can tell you which letter occurs more often, calculate the fraction of A tickets, or choose the score that minimizes either loss in that column. Changing the question I asked the notebook cost me a fresh calculation when I read it. The instruction to add one to the count still worked. On the first page of this book, the state of the learner was a distribution, and the rule that updated it was called ℱ . The notebook has grown. At one point it held counts and at another it held the coefficients of a line. If S t is what we keep, d t the new datum, and Q the question, we now have room for two operations, S t = U ( S t − 1 ; d t ) , answer = R Q ( S t ) . When the state is a distribution over hypotheses, U can be our ℱ , and R Q can simply read off the probability of A. We needed the distinction once we could ask the same state different questions and give the same datum to rules that handle it differently. What I Chose Before Opening the Notebook To place a bet. In logistic regression, I choose the features that make up the log odds and charge according to the probability given to the letter that was revealed. Before I use the result as a risk, I want to see how often errors occur among the parts whose fate depends on that risk. To separate. With an SVM, I choose a representation, a ruler for measuring distance, and a price for margin violations. A correctly classified example beyond the margin has already paid its share of the loss. The pile with nine A tickets and one B ticket is still on the table. You know only those counts and you bet according to the observed frequency. I bring another ticket with matching faces. We turn it over. B. You cross out the ten at the bottom of the column and write eleven. I ask about the next letter. You say A, just as you did before. I hold out the ticket that pays ten reais and ask R$ 8.80 for it. It is now worth 10 × 9 / 11 to you, about R$ 8.18. You leave my hand hanging there. If I had written down only the letter you predicted, I could have spent the whole afternoon without noticing that you had learned something. Corinna Cortes and Vladimir Vapnik develop the classifier with a margin and margin violations in Support-Vector Networks (1995). For the formulation in terms of a loss and a penalty, see T. Hastie, S. Rosset, R. Tibshirani, and J. Zhu, The Entire Regularization Path for the Support Vector Machine (2004). ↩︎

title: How Much Does 90% Weigh?
text: Let’s go back one ticket in time. You still have the nine A’s and one B from the end of the last chapter. I’ve been collecting tickets with matching faces too, only I started earlier. My notebook has ninety A’s and ten B’s. We agree to use the observed frequency to bet on which machine will print the next ticket with matching faces. Ask us what probability we give A. Each of us writes 90 % on a slip of paper. The ticket costs R$ 8.80 and pays ten reais if it comes from A. We both put its expected payout at nine reais. We buy. Another ticket with matching faces comes in. The label says B. We write down the same letter. What’s the next ticket worth? Your estimate has fallen to 9 / 11 , so the ticket is now worth about R$ 8.18 to you. You pass. Mine has fallen to 90 / 101 . At the same price of R$ 8.80, I’m still buying something I expect to be worth R$ 8.91. Suppose all I collected yesterday was the two slips of paper. Today I write the function from the first page. I try it with your bet from yesterday and the new observation. The inputs are 90 % and B. I try it with mine. The inputs are 90 % and B. What line of code could possibly tell whose slip it was? The Part of the Calculation That Disappeared When we summarized the history by its frequency, we did a division. Nine divided by ten gives the same number as ninety divided by a hundred. That’s exactly what we wanted when we compared the bets. But what operation did the new B ask us to perform? Add one to the denominator. That’s when we needed to know what we’d divided by. Let n be the number of entries and q the fraction of them that are A. The number of A’s is n q . Write t = 1 if the new letter is A and t = 0 if it’s B. Before doing the division, try to predict which way the number will move. If the new entry contributed exactly the old average q , the average would stay put. It contributed t . The excess or shortfall is t − q , and we now spread that difference over n + 1 entries. We can count letters or spread out the difference. The two calculations give q ′ = n q + t n + 1 = q + t − q n + 1 . The term t − q is − 0.9 in both notebooks. How far does the observation move the bet? You divide that term by 11 . I divide it by 101 . If each of us had written q and n on our slip, I could have done both calculations. I’d even know what to keep for tomorrow, since the new state is ( q ′ , n + 1 ) . I’m counting rounds here. If my hundred entries were ten photocopies of each of your ten, we’d still have seen only ten rounds. To decide how much weight to give a notebook, you also need to know who filled it. Could we program a learner that keeps only q ? Sure. Give the latest entry one tenth of the weight every time and write q ′ = q + ( t − q ) / 10 . Both slips marked 90 % will now give 81 % after a B. If I want recent rounds to carry more weight because a machine’s setting can change, I have a reason to try that rule. But I’ve just made a choice about the learner. With a hundred entries in my notebook, the observed frequency would give the next one a weight of 1 / 101 . Giving it a tenth needs a reason of its own. A Test for Any Notebook Let h stand for the history the learner has read, and S ( h ) for what it kept. Write h d for the history we get by adding the observation d at the end. Assume we can give the program the same set of possible observations after any history. In our game I can hand you an A or a B. I want to close the file of old records and still get exactly the state tomorrow that I’d get if I reopened the file and worked through everything again. In other words, I want a deterministic rule U such that U ( S ( h ) , d ) = S ( h d ) . Choose two histories that the summary treats as indistinguishable. Close the notebooks and give both of them the same new letter. Your program gets precisely the same inputs. If you open the notebooks and find two different next states, which one was the program supposed to write down? That’s the test this arrow expresses. S ( h ) = S ( h ′ ) ⇒ S ( h d ) = S ( h ′ d ) for every d . A rule U with the property we want exists if and only if the summary passes this test for every pair of histories. If U exists, it gets identical inputs in the two cases and can give only one answer. That’s how we found the flaw in our two slips marked 90 % . What about the other direction? Suppose the summary always passes the test. To define U ( s , d ) for a state s we can actually reach, choose any history h that leads to s , append d , and return S ( h d ) . Could someone with a different notebook ending in s object to that instruction? By the test, all those notebooks call for the same answer. We have our rule. We can apply it again next round, and keep going. There’s a way to cheat on this test. Write zero on the slip, whatever happens. The rule that returns zero passes with flying colors. Now try getting a price for the ticket out of it. We’re missing the other half of the problem. Fix a question Q and call A Q ( h ) the answer our method would give with the whole notebook at hand. For us to read that answer from the summary, two histories with the same S must also give the same answer A Q . If that’s true, we can call the readout R Q and write A Q ( h ) = R Q ( S ( h ) ) . The slip marked 90 % could give yesterday’s price and lost track when B arrived. The slip marked zero can keep a calculation going forever without ever telling us what to pay. The Other Slip Marked 90% If the number of observations mattered so much, how did we manage to toss a coin all through Chapter 1 without carrying the count around in Bayes’ formula? Go back to the drawer. Coin A lands heads with probability 3 / 4 and coin B with probability 1 / 4 . We know the rates. We choose one coin at random with equal chances and keep it for the whole round. One table records two heads. Another records three heads and one tail. At both tables the odds in favor of A are nine to one. An extra head and an extra tail undo each other’s effect. Here are our two slips marked 90 % again. Let’s test them. I reveal a tail at each table. A tail is three times as likely under B as under A. On both slips the odds go from nine to one to three to one, and the probability of A falls to 3 / 4 . A head, in turn, would have tripled the odds at both tables. Once we’ve fixed which coin we have, each toss is independent of the ones before it. Any sequence to come will therefore have the same effect on both bets. For this drawer, knowing today’s odds is enough to update the odds tomorrow. In the first two notebooks, 90 % was an estimate of the frequency of A in a population, and the new B was one more observation from that population. At the drawer, 90 % is our bet on the identity of the coin I’m already holding, and the new observation is a face that coin produced. In one case we need to revise the rate we’ll use for the next ticket. In the other, the rate of heads for each type of coin was part of the rules from the start. This is the promise we made in Chapter 1 when we wrote p t = ℱ ( p t − 1 ; x t ) . To keep it, we need to choose what the distribution is over and know how the next observation relates to what we kept. What a Summary Needs to Preserve To answer. Histories leading to the same state must agree on the answers to the questions the program will have to handle. To keep going. Give the same next observation to two histories that reached the same state. If the method calls for two different next states, something we needed was on the paper we threw away. In the coin notebook we cut into pieces, two histories with the same sixty heads in eighty tosses give the same estimate of 3 / 4 . Ask how often two heads came together, and swapping two pieces is enough to make the histories disagree. With the printers, a first head and a first tail both leave our bet on the machine at 1 / 2 . Open the second window and you discover why we needed to remember the first. Even the value of an observation depends on the job at hand. When the drawer gives either coin an equal chance, peeking at the first toss tells us, on average, 0.189 bits about the coin’s identity, as we worked out in Chapter 2. How much would you pay me for that peek if all you could do with the result was decide whether to buy a ticket paying ten reais if the coin is A? At two reais a ticket, you’d buy before peeking and still buy if you saw tails, when your probability for A fell to 1 / 4 . The peek is worth zero reais for that decision. Now I raise the price to five reais. If you see heads, you buy a ticket with an expected payout of R$ 7.50. If you see tails, you sit it out. Before seeing the toss, your expected gain was zero. Getting to choose after you look is worth ( 1 / 2 ) ( 7.50 − 5 ) = 1.25 reais on average. Did I do anything to the coin to change the price of that information? Back in the workshop, the generative model and logistic regression could give the same odds on the machine. Only the first could simulate a production run. The SVM score was enough to operate the sorting gate. Pricing the risk on a part took calibration. On the first page, you offered me eighty centavos if the coin landed heads and sixty if it landed tails for a ticket you’d just sold me for fifty. We found the mistake before tossing the coin. Our hypothesis was this. To learn is to keep our bets coherent as new data arrive. Now we have two tests for that idea. When the numbers are prices, I can write out a single ticket and price it two ways. When I run the program, I can give it two pasts it summarized in the same way and ask it to honor the bets it promised for the next round. The first test checks the model’s arithmetic. The second checks whether the learner kept what it needs to do that arithmetic. There’s still a check neither one can do for me. If the model assumes independence where the machine copies the first face, it can pass both tests and keep losing money. I need to open fresh tickets. The Workshop Changes Its Mind The next day the inspector has a small request. He suspects the machine’s setting has begun to drift and wants the display to show the fraction of A’s in the last three tickets only . I show him two notebooks, with the letters in the order they came in, A A B A B A . Both give 2 / 3 . The inspector knows he’ll have to drop the oldest letter. He suggests keeping ( 2 / 3 , A ) in each device, the fraction on the display and the letter to drop next. He challenges me to make the display give the wrong answer. I bring a B. Once we drop the first letter, the windows become A B B and B A B . The fraction of A’s falls to 1 / 3 in both. The inspector smiles. I bring another B. The first window now holds three B’s. The second still has one A. The displays ought to read zero and 1 / 3 . Look back at the round when both still read 1 / 3 . Even then, the first device needed to remember A as the next letter to go, while the second needed to remember B. Given identical starting notes and the same observation, how could the program have written down two different letters? If it keeps all three letters in order, it can drop the one on the left and add the new one on the right. Being asked to forget the old ones is what made their order worth remembering. The error showed up on the display one round after the learner forgot what it needed to honor its next bet. That’s how I’d try to break a learner before putting it into production. I’d give it two pasts it had chosen to forget in the same way. Then I’d look for the observation that would make it wish it had kept the difference.
